title: Direct object pronouns
description: mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le — position, elision and agreement in the passato prossimo.
objectives: Replace a direct object noun with the right pronoun.
Place the pronoun before the verb or attach it to an infinitive.
Make the participle agree after lo, la, li, le.
Use ne for quantities and for di + something.

blocks.title: The pronoun replaces the whole noun phrase
blocks.text: *Vedo il gatto → Lo vedo. Mangio la mela → La mangio. Chiamo i bambini → Li chiamo. Guardo le stelle → Le guardo.* Gender and number come from the noun replaced.

blocks.title: Before the conjugated verb
blocks.text: *Lo vedo. Non lo vedo. Ti chiamo domani.*

blocks.title: Attached to an infinitive
blocks.text: The infinitive loses its final -e: *vedere + lo → vederlo*. With modals either position works: *Lo voglio vedere = Voglio vederlo.*

blocks.title: Elision before avere
blocks.text: *lo* and *la* usually elide before a vowel or h: *l'ho visto, l'ha presa*. *li* and *le* do not: *li ho visti*.

blocks.title: Agreement with lo, la, li, le
blocks.text: When *lo, la, li, le* come before *avere*, the participle agrees with the pronoun: *Hai visto la volpe? — Sì, l'ho vista. Hai visto i gufi? — Sì, li ho visti. Le stelle? — Le ho guardate.*

blocks.title: Optional with mi, ti, ci, vi
blocks.text: With *mi, ti, ci, vi* agreement is optional: *Sara, ti ho vista / ti ho visto.*

blocks.title: Not with indirect objects
blocks.text: There is no agreement with indirect object pronouns: *Hai scritto a Sara? — Sì, le ho scritto.* For the complete rules (ne, reflexive verbs, relative che, modal verbs) see [[ausiliari-accordo|auxiliaries and agreement]].

blocks.title: Partitive ne: a quantity of something
blocks.text: *ne* replaces a noun when you mention a quantity of it, or none: *Quante mele hai? — Ne ho tre. Vuoi del pane? — No, grazie, non ne voglio.* The number or quantity stays in the sentence; *ne* replaces the noun. English often has nothing: 'I have three (of them)'.

blocks.title: ne = di + something
blocks.text: *ne* also replaces *di* + a thing or idea: *Ne parliamo domani* (we will talk about it tomorrow), *Che ne pensi?* (what do you think of it?). Less often it replaces *da* + a place: *Ne è uscito* (he came out of it).

blocks.title: Position
blocks.text: Like the other unstressed pronouns, *ne* goes before a finite verb and is attached to an infinitive, a gerund or an affirmative imperative (tu, noi, voi): *Voglio comprarne due. Prendine uno!* With *c'è / ci sono*: *ce n'è uno, ce ne sono tre*.

blocks.title: Agreement
blocks.text: In compound tenses the participle normally agrees with the noun ne replaces: *Di mele, ne ho mangiate tre.* The invariable *mangiato* is also found.

examples.it: Dov'è il gatto? — Non lo vedo.
examples.en: Where's the cat? — I can't see it.
The apple? I'll eat it.

examples.en: Mum calls the children and takes them home.

examples.it: Hai visto la volpe? — Sì, l'ho vista.
examples.en: Did you see the fox? — Yes, I saw it.

examples.it: Quanti fratelli hai? — Ne ho due.
examples.en: How many brothers do you have? — I have two.

mistakes.message: gli is an indirect object pronoun ('to him/to them'). The direct object 'them' (masculine) is li.

exercises.explanation: la elides before ho, and the participle agrees with la: vista.

mistakes.message: The pronoun la (la volpe) is feminine, so the participle agrees: l'ho vista.

exercises.explanation: vedere loses -e and takes lo: vederlo.
Before a verb, la is an object pronoun; before a noun (la mela) it is the article.

exercises.prompt: Complete with ne or a direct object pronoun.
exercises.text: Quante torte fai? — {0} faccio due. Il libro? {1} leggo stasera.
exercises.explanation: A quantity (due) → ne; the whole definite object (il libro) → lo.

exercises.prompt: Answer with ne and the passato prossimo: *Quante mele hai mangiato?* (tre) → ___ tre.
exercises.explanation: With ne the participle normally agrees with the noun (mele → mangiate); the invariable form is also found.

summary: mi, ti, lo/la, ci, vi, li/le replace the direct object.
Before the conjugated verb (after non); attached to an infinitive (vederlo).
lo/la elide before avere (l'ho); the participle agrees with lo, la, li, le.
ne replaces a noun after a quantity (ne ho tre) or di + something (ne parliamo); its position is like the other pronouns.

title: Indirect object pronouns
description: mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, gli — 'to me, to him…', with dare, dire, piacere.
objectives: Use indirect object pronouns with verbs of giving and saying.
Combine indirect and direct pronouns (me lo, glielo).

blocks.title: Replacing a + person
blocks.text: An indirect object pronoun replaces *a* + a person: *Do un regalo a Marco → Gli do un regalo. Scrivo a Sara → Le scrivo.*

blocks.title: 'To them'
blocks.text: In everyday Italian *gli* also means 'to them': *Gli parlo domani*. The formal alternative is *loro* after the verb: *Parlo loro domani*.

sections.heading: Verbs that take an indirect object

items: *dare, portare, regalare* (to give something to someone)
*dire, raccontare, scrivere, rispondere, telefonare* (to say / write / reply to someone)
*piacere, sembrare* (to please, to seem to someone)

blocks.title: Different from English
blocks.text: Some verbs take a direct object in Italian where English has 'to' or 'for': *ascoltare la musica* (listen to music), *aspettare il treno* (wait for the train), *cercare la chiave* (look for the key). Others take an indirect object where English has none: *telefonare a Sara → le telefono* (I phone her).

blocks.title: Indirect + direct
blocks.text: When an indirect pronoun and *lo, la, li, le* or *ne* occur together, the indirect one comes first and its -i becomes -e: *mi → me, ti → te, ci → ce, vi → ve, si → se*. *Mi dai il libro? → Me lo dai? Ti porto le mele → Te le porto.*

blocks.title: glielo
blocks.text: *gli* and *le* (to him, to her, to you formal) both become *glie-* and are written as one word with the following pronoun: *glielo, gliela, glieli, gliele, gliene*. *Do il libro a Marco / a Sara → Glielo do.* Context shows who receives it.

blocks.title: Position and agreement
blocks.text: The pair behaves like a single pronoun: before a finite verb, attached to an infinitive, gerund or affirmative imperative (*Puoi darmelo? Dammelo!*). In compound tenses the participle agrees with the direct object pronoun: *Le chiavi? Gliele ho date.*

examples.it: Il nonno ci racconta una storia.
examples.en: Grandfather tells us a story.

examples.it: Le chiavi? Gliele ho già date.
examples.en: The keys? I've already given them to him / her.
examples.note: glie- + le; date agrees with le.

summary: mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli replace a + person.
gli = to him (and colloquially to them); le = to her; Le = to you (formal).
ascoltare, aspettare, cercare take direct objects; telefonare, rispondere, piacere take indirect ones.
Combined pronouns: me lo, te la, glielo, ce ne …; indirect first, -i → -e, gli/le → glie-.

title: Relative clauses, adverbs and expressions in stories
description: che and cui; adverbs in -mente; infinitive constructions; idioms you meet in children's stories.
objectives: Join sentences with the relative pronouns che and cui.
Recognise infinitive constructions and common narrative expressions.

blocks.title: che = who, which, that (subject or direct object)
blocks.text: *Il ragazzo che canta è mio fratello.* (subject) — *Il libro che leggo è bello.* (object). *che* is invariable and, unlike English 'that', can never be omitted.

blocks.title: cui after a preposition
blocks.text: After a preposition use *cui*: *la casa in cui abito* (the house I live in), *l'amica con cui gioco* (the friend I play with), *il ragazzo a cui scrivo* (the boy I'm writing to).

blocks.title: il quale
blocks.text: *il quale, la quale, i quali, le quali* can replace *che* or *cui*, and agree in gender and number with the antecedent: *la ragazza con la quale parlavo* = *la ragazza con cui parlavo*. They are typical of formal or written style, and useful to avoid ambiguity, because the article shows which noun is meant: *la sorella di Marco, la quale vive a Roma* (the sister lives in Rome). After a preposition the article contracts: *del quale, alla quale, nei quali*. As the subject or object of a restrictive relative clause, *che* is normal and *il quale* sounds heavy or bureaucratic.

blocks.title: Feminine singular + -mente
blocks.text: *lento → lenta → lentamente*; *veloce → velocemente*. Adjectives in *-le* and *-re* drop the final e: *gentile → gentilmente, regolare → regolarmente*.

blocks.title: Irregular adverbs
blocks.text: *buono → bene*, *cattivo → male*. Many common adverbs do not end in -mente: *presto, tardi, sempre, piano, insieme, subito*.

items: Verb + *a* + infinitive: *cominciare a, imparare a, aiutare a* — *Comincia a piovere.*
Verb + *di* + infinitive: *cercare di* (to try to), *decidere di, finire di* — *Cerca di dormire.*
*per* + infinitive = in order to: *Esce per giocare.*

blocks.caption: Expressions common in children's stories
rows: Once upon a time there was…
and they lived happily ever after (passato remoto of vivere, the standard tense of fairy-tale narration)
